replacements.value: The con case could turn its general historical criteria into a source-by-source audit of the alleged six resurrection witnesses. For each source, it should identify date, authorship, genre, access to eyewitnesses, theological interests, literary dependence, and any details unlikely to derive from a shared tradition. It could then discount claims that are repeated but not independently attested and compare the residue with ordinary explanations such as memory distortion or legendary development. This would show why numerical multiplicity is not automatically corroboration without dismissing testimony as intrinsically worthless.

Hiddenness could be framed as a comparative prediction rather than as a claim about what God is obligated to do. If a loving, communicative God seeks relationship with people, then sincere inquiry should often converge on recognizable access to that God, even though knowledge would not compel worship or loyalty. By contrast, persistent disagreement that tracks culture and remains among nonresistant inquirers is more expected if religions arise through ordinary human processes. The con case could therefore treat hiddenness as positive likelihood evidence against Christianity, while allowing that isolated ambiguity may serve other purposes.
